project_tracker_diagnostic: Perennial ragweed; lower leaves opposite and upper leaves alternate; blades toothed to pinnately lobed; often forms colonies from spreading roots/rhizomes.

project_inclusion.learning_reason: Common, conspicuous, or high-value comparison species for Central Texas field ID.

morphology_keys.leaves: Lower leaves opposite, upper alternate; deltate to lanceolate, pinnately toothed to 1-pinnately lobed.
morphology_keys.flowers: Male heads in terminal spike-like racemes; female heads clustered below.
morphology_keys.fruit: Small obpyramidal to globose burs with 0–6 short distal spines/tubercles.
best_field_traits: Perennial often forming connected patches from creeping rhizomes; check underground connections only where disturbance is appropriate
Lower leaves commonly opposite, upper alternate; blades toothed to deeply lobed, but leaf form varies
Terminal elongated clusters of pollen-bearing male heads; small seed-bearing female heads occur below, toward leaf axils
Compare annual Ambrosia artemisiifolia: often more finely dissected foliage and no persistent perennial rhizome network; leaf shape alone can overlap
Compare giant ragweed A. trifida: much larger broad 3–5-lobed leaves and tall coarse stems; inspect reproductive heads for confirmation

photo_strategy.selection_logic: Prefer curated taxon photos plus multiple views from one Central Texas/Texas observation.
photo_strategy.remaining_need: NEEDS_DIAGNOSTIC_PHOTO: close-up female seed-bearing heads/burs with scale and safely exposed rhizome connection. annotation_pending until exact photographed structures and rights are verified.

field_id_lesson.look_here_first: Check lower opposite versus upper alternate leaves, then terminal drooping-to-upright clusters of pollen-bearing male heads. Search just below these spikes and in upper leaf axils for the much smaller female heads. Do not identify from leaf lobing alone.
crew_checkpoints: Habit: erect perennial, frequently in colonies; rhizomes are supporting evidence only when already exposed, not a reason to dig up managed sites.
Leaves: lower opposite and upper alternate; variable toothed to pinnately lobed blades. Photograph both nodes and a complete blade.
Flowers: terminal racemes of small male heads, with separate female heads lower down near upper leaf axils. Photograph both on the same plant.
Fruit: burs may have 0–6 short spines or tubercles; photograph mature fruit beside a millimeter scale before relying on this trait.

local_look_alikes.distinguish: Annual common ragweed typically has more finely dissected foliage; check perennial rhizome evidence and flowering structures rather than leaf form alone.
Giant ragweed usually has much larger broad leaves, often with 3–5 palmate lobes, unlike the narrower pinnately lobed leaves here.
